extra.message: pickle.loads() on line 52 deserializes user-controlled input from request body (or query param if 'blob' is provided) without any integrity checks. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary code upon deserialization, leading to Remote Code Execution.

os.system() on line 124 concatenates the user-controlled 'host' query parameter directly into a shell command 'ping -c 1 ' + host. An attacker can inject shell metacharacters (e.g., '; rm -rf /') to execute arbitrary system commands.

urllib.request.urlopen() on line 87 takes the user-controlled 'endpoint' query parameter directly without validation. An attacker can supply internal URLs (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ for AWS metadata, or http://localhost:6379/) to perform Server-Side Request Forgery.

lxml XMLParser on line 137 is configured with resolve_entities=True and no_network=False. User-controlled XML from the request body is parsed with DTD loading and entity resolution enabled, allowing XXE attacks to read local files or cause SSRF.

Jinja2 Template on line 110 is constructed by directly concatenating the user-controlled 'fragment' query parameter into the template string and calling render(). Since HTMLResponse returns the result to the client (CWE-79), but more critically an attacker could inject Jinja2 expressions like {{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read() }} to achieve Remote Code Execution.

On line 69, the tenant-stash endpoint writes SSN and credit card data to disk. The key 'ssn' with default '111-22-3333' and 'card' with default '4111111111111111' are hardcoded placeholder PII that would be stored on the filesystem accessible to anyone with server access.

cwe: CWE-359: Exposure of Private Personal Information

extra.message: On line 39, RedirectResponse takes the user-controlled 'lane' query parameter directly without validation. An attacker can craft a link to this endpoint redirecting users to any external domain (e.g., https://evil.com/phishing) for phishing attacks.

Lines 103-104 explicitly clear security headers: X-XSS-Protection is set to '0' (disabling browser XSS filter) and Content-Security-Policy is set to empty string. Combined with SSTI on this endpoint, removing CSP enables XSS attacks that would otherwise be mitigated.
On line 36, session cookie is set with secure=False, meaning it will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. This allows session hijacking via network sniffing on any non-HTTPS connection.

cwe: CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in Session Cookie Without 'Secure' Attribute

extra.message: DEMO_PASSWORD = 'Password123!' is a hardcoded plaintext password used for all seed user accounts. This credential is printed in plain text at line 218 when the script runs, and all demo accounts share the same weak password.

Lines 210 and 220 create an API key with known plaintext value 'pm_demo_status_key'. This key is printed in plain text to stdout on line 220, making it trivially discoverable by anyone who can run the seed script or read its output logs.

The password_reset/request endpoint returns differentiated responses: if a user exists, a reset token is generated and written to a file; if not, it still returns 'ok: True'. The consistent response body makes timing attacks possible to enumerate registered email addresses.

CORS middleware on lines 84-90 allows all origins (via settings.cors_origin wildcard + allow_methods=['*'] and allow_headers=['*']) with credentials enabled. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests, enabling CSRF-style attacks against APIs.

hashlib.md5() on line 77 uses the weak MD5 hashing algorithm. While not directly exploitable for RCE here (it computes a digest of a user-provided phrase), MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks. If used for integrity verification, an attacker could craft inputs that produce the same hash.

Default database_url on line 8 contains hardcoded credentials 'postgres:postgres@localhost:55440'. If the .env file is missing or not loaded, this default is used, exposing the database password in the source code.

The trace endpoint on lines 142-144 publicly exposes the APP_ENV environment variable and the base export directory path to any authenticated caller. Internal deployment details like cloud provider (e.g., 'staging' vs 'production') can be leaked, aiding further attacks.

The /dock endpoint on line 114 accepts a 'name' parameter (defaulting to 'packet.bin') and writes the request body directly to BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name. While there is a default value, an attacker can control both filename and content, potentially overwriting system files or filling disk space.

On lines 149-152, the MongoDB query is derived entirely from user-controlled request body (payload['filter'] or entire payload). An attacker can inject arbitrary MongoDB query operators ({ $where, $regex }) to perform NoSQL injection attacks, potentially exfiltrating all database records.
On line 786, CSV import of users with default password 'TenantPass123!' creates all imported accounts with the same hardcoded password. No password strength validation is performed on imported rows.
